content: Vertebrates are members of the subphylum Vertebrata, which are chordates characterized by the presence of a backbone or spinal column. Although hagfish lack vertebrae, they are genetically closely related to lampreys, which do possess vertebrae. For this reason, the subphylum is sometimes referred to as Craniata, as all members have a cranium. Approximately 58,000 species of vertebrates have been identified. Vertebrata is the largest subphylum within chordates and includes many well-known groups of large terrestrial animals. Vertebrates encompass cyclostomes (jawless fish), bony fish, sharks and rays, amphibians, reptiles, mammals, and birds. Their size ranges from the tiny Paedophryne amauensis (measuring about 7.7 mm) to the massive blue whale, which can reach up to 33 meters in length. One defining feature of vertebrates is their muscular system, which primarily consists of paired muscle masses. They also possess a central nervous system, part of which is housed within the backbone, if present. The hallmark characteristics of vertebrates include the presence of a backbone or spinal cord, a braincase, and an internal skeleton. However, these features are not universally applicable; for instance, lampreys lack an internal skeleton, and some other chordates may exhibit a rudimentary spinal cord. Vertebrates are most easily distinguished from other chordates by their well-defined head, which contains concentrated sensory organs, particularly eyes, at the anterior end of the body. This pronounced cephalization contrasts with organisms like lancelets, which have a mouth but lack a fully developed head and instead have light-sensitive areas distributed along their back. Vertebrates originated approximately 500 million years ago during the Cambrian explosion, a significant evolutionary event within the Cambrian period. The earliest known vertebrate is Myllokunmingia. Recent molecular analyses suggest that hagfish (Myxini) also belong to Vertebrata, although some researchers consider them a sister group to vertebrates within the broader taxon Craniata. The earliest fossil evidence of vertebrates includes Myllokunmingia fengjiaoa and Haikouichthys ercaicunensis, which date back to approximately 513–542 million years ago during the Early Cambrian period. These fossils were discovered in Yunnan, China. The classification of vertebrates, as proposed by Janvier (1981, 1997), Shu et al. (2003), and Benton (2004), includes the following groups: Subphylum Vertebrata (unranked group) Hyperoartia (lampreys) Class †Conodonta Subclass †Pteraspidomorphi Class †Thelodonti Class †Anaspida Class †Galeaspida Class †Pituriaspida Class †Osteostraci Infraphylum Gnathostomata (jawed vertebrates) Class †Placodermi (Paleozoic armored forms) Class Chondrichthyes (cartilaginous fish) Class †Acanthodii (Paleozoic spiny sharks) Superclass Osteichthyes (bony fish) Class Actinopterygii (ray-finned fish) Class Sarcopterygii (lobe-finned fish) Subclass Coelacanthimorpha (coelacanths) Subclass Dipnoi (lungfish) Subclass Tetrapodomorpha (ancestral to tetrapods) Superclass Tetrapoda (four-limbed vertebrates) Class Amphibia (amphibians) Series Amniota (amniotic embryo) Class Sauropsida (reptiles and birds) Class Aves (birds) Class Synapsida (mammal-like reptiles) Class Mammalia (mammals) The term vertebrate is derived from the Latin word vertebrātus (as used by Pliny), meaning having joints. It is closely related to the word vertebra, which refers to any of the bones or segments that make up the spinal column.
